mn59:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn59:1.3: Then the Carpenter Pañcakanga went to the venerable Udāyin, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked him:
mn59:1.4: ‘Venerable sir, how many kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One?’
mn59:1.5: ‘Three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder:
mn59:1.6: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
mn59:1.7: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’
mn59:1.8: When this was said, the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:
mn59:1.9: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;
mn59:1.10: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:
mn59:1.12: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’
mn59:2.1: A second time the venerable Udāyin said to the carpenter Pañcakanga:
mn59:2.2: ‘Not two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder;
mn59:2.3: three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:
mn59:2.4: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
mn59:2.5: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’
mn59:2.6: A second time the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:
mn59:2.7: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;
mn59:2.8: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:
mn59:2.10: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’
mn59:3.1: A third time the venerable Udāyin said to the carpenter Pañcakanga:
mn59:3.2: ‘Not two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder;
mn59:3.3: three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:
mn59:3.4: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
mn59:3.5: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’
mn59:3.6: A third time the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:
mn59:3.7: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;
mn59:3.8: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:
mn59:3.10: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’
mn59:3.11: The venerable Udāyin could not make the carpenter Pañcakanga perceive, nor could the carpenter Pañcakanga make the venerable Udāyin perceive.
mn59:4.1: The venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the venerable Udāyin and the carpenter Pañcakanga.
mn59:4.2: Then he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.
mn59:4.3: When he had done so, he reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation between the venerable Udāyin and Pañcakanga the carpenter.
mn59:4.4: When this was said, the Blessed One told the venerable Ānanda:
mn59:5.1: ‘Ānanda, it was actually a true presentation that Pañcakanga the carpenter would not accept from Udāyin, and it was actually a true presentation that Udāyin would not accept from Pañcakanga the carpenter.
mn59:5.2: I have stated two kinds of feeling in one presentation, Ānanda; I have stated three kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated five kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated six kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated eighteen kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated thirty-six kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated one hundred and eight kinds of feeling in another presentation.
mn59:5.3: That is how the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations.
mn59:5.4: And when the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations thus, it may be expected of those who will not concede, allow and accept what is well-stated, well-spoken, by each that they will abide quarrelling, brawling and disputing, stabbing each other with verbal daggers.
mn59:5.5: That is how the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations.
mn59:5.6: And when the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations thus, it may be expected of those who concede, allow and accept what is well-stated, well-spoken, by each that they will abide in concord as friendly and undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.
mn59:6.1: ‘Ānanda, there are these five cords of sensual desire.
mn59:6.3: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust,
mn59:6.7: tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust—
mn59:6.8: these, Ānanda, are the five cords of sensual desire.
mn59:6.9: Now, Ānanda, the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five cords of sensual desire is called pleasure in sensual desires.
mn59:7.1: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.
mn59:7.3: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:7.4: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:7.5: Here, Ānanda, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna.
mn59:7.6: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:8.1: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.
mn59:8.3: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:8.4: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:8.5: Here, Ānanda, with the stilling of initial and sustained application … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna.
mn59:8.6: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:9.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:9.4: Here, Ānanda, with the fading of happiness … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the third jhāna.
mn59:9.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:10.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:10.4: Here, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.
mn59:10.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:11.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:11.4: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of variety, aware that ‘space is infinite’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of infinite space.
mn59:11.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:12.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:12.4: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of infinite consciousness.
mn59:12.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:13.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:13.4: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.
mn59:13.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:14.3: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:14.4: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn59:14.5: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:15.1: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.
mn59:15.3: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:15.4: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?
mn59:15.5: Here, Ānanda, by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling.
mn59:15.6: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.
mn59:16.1: ‘An instance might be found, Ānanda, of Wanderers of other sects saying thus:
mn59:16.2: “The monk Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling and describes that as pleasure:
mn59:16.3: What is this, and how is this?”
mn59:16.4: Wanderers of other sects who say thus, Ānanda, should be told:
mn59:16.5: ‘Friends, the Blessed One describes pleasure with reference not only to pleasant feeling;
mn59:16.6: rather, friends, a Tathāgata describes as pleasure any kind of pleasure wherever and whereinsoever it is obtained.’”
mn59:16.7: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn59:16.8: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
